text: Accepted runtime baselines should be centralized in a small helper module to avoid scattered fixed-count assumptions across the test suite. When each smoke test hardcodes its own expected JSONL record counts and FAISS id totals, accepted memory growth forces redundant repairs in multiple files. A single helper such as tests/smoke/_accepted_runtime_baseline.py stores the current front identifier, commit short hash, and canonical counts. Tests import this helper and assert against its values rather than embedding stale numbers. When a new ingestion front advances memory, updating one helper propagates the baseline to all consumers. This pattern was validated in the 09B closeout where three legacy tests were aligned by referencing a shared baseline, proving maintainability and reducing future repair burden.
summary: Centralize accepted baselines in a single helper to avoid scattered assumptions

text: Legacy tests should preserve historical report artifact assertions while checking live memory against the current accepted baseline. The 08F batch promotion test still validates that the 08F manifest contains exactly twenty-four candidates, that candidate IDs are unique, and that text hashes are unique. These assertions remain correct regardless of later memory growth. However, the same test previously asserted that current live counts equal the 08F post-promotion counts, which breaks after 09A and 09B. The correct repair keeps the historical assertions intact and adds a current-baseline assertion. This demonstrates that historical front reports are immutable evidence while live memory is an evolving runtime state. Tests must distinguish between verifying a historical event and asserting the present system state.
summary: Preserve historical artifact assertions while aligning live checks to current baseline

text: Read-only tests should use dynamic before-and-after SHA comparison instead of hardcoded old SHA values. The FAISS rebuild hydration test originally compared semantic_memory.jsonl against a SHA from a pre-09A baseline. Any subsequent promotion mutated the file and invalidated the hardcoded SHA, causing false failures. The repair computes the SHA immediately before the read-only inspection, runs the inspection, then recomputes the SHA and asserts equality. This proves the test action did not mutate JSONL without requiring knowledge of future file contents. Dynamic SHA invariants are future-proof because they depend only on local file state, not on external baselines that change with every ingestion cycle. The same pattern applies to any read-only integrity check on mutable runtime files.
summary: Use dynamic before/after SHA instead of hardcoded old SHA in read-only tests

text: After accepted memory growth shifts baselines, full regression must confirm no functional regressions and no unintended memory mutation. The 09B closeout repaired three legacy tests and then executed the complete regression suite spanning auth endpoints, memory hygiene, 08F batch promotion, 08B promotion tool, semantic retrieval, and the new 09B tests. All tests passed, proving that the baseline shift was purely additive with no degradation of existing functionality. Running the full suite after any ingestion front is mandatory because promotion tools, retrieval paths, and agent behavior are interconnected. A failure in auth tests after an ingestion front would indicate a cross-cutting regression even if memory counts appear correct. Regression results should be recorded in a JSON artifact for traceability.
summary: Full regression after baseline shift confirms no functional regressions

text: Medium-batch ingestion is authorized only after three-record and twelve-record end-to-end stages have been proven successful. The ingestion scaling ladder requires each stage to validate promotion, retrieval, agent-use probes, rollback safety, and Git hygiene before advancing to the next size. The 09A front proved three curated candidates could be promoted and retrieved. The 09B front proved twelve candidates with the same safety invariants. A twenty-four candidate medium batch is the logical next increment. Skipping stages risks overwhelming validation pipelines, exceeding snapshot storage, and making failure diagnosis difficult. Each stage also refines quality thresholds and embedding behavior under realistic but limited load. Governance must enforce this ladder because the approval token itself should only be issued after the previous stage is complete.
summary: Medium-batch ingestion requires prior 3-record and 12-record E2E success

text: Batch ingestion fronts must enforce exact candidate counts before validation and promotion. The 09B front specified exactly twelve candidates with explicit candidate IDs, topics, and word-count constraints. The 09C front scales to exactly twenty-four candidates. Count enforcement prevents scope creep during front execution and ensures the validation gate checks the intended batch size. If the actual candidate count deviates from the specification, the front must halt with a validation failure. This gate is checked by asserting total_candidates equals the planned count and that valid_candidates and promotable_candidates match. Exact counts also simplify post-promotion verification because the expected JSONL and FAISS increments are known in advance. Operators should not approve promotion tokens until the candidate manifest has been manually reviewed and locked.
summary: Batch fronts must enforce exact candidate counts before validation

text: Controlled ingestion must use safe local reports only and must not ingest arbitrary internet content or raw runtime logs. The allowed source pool for 09B and 09C consists of front final reports, batch summaries, validation artifacts, and test files already produced by the system. These sources are known, bounded, and contain concise operational lessons rather than bulk data. Ingesting arbitrary internet pages would introduce unvetted content, unknown domains, and potential secrets. Ingesting raw stdout or stderr would bloat the index with transient log lines that have no semantic value. The front specification explicitly lists permitted sources and instructs operators to skip missing files rather than search the internet. This boundary preserves the quality of canonical memory and prevents contamination from external or ephemeral data.
summary: Controlled ingestion must use safe local reports only, not internet or raw logs

text: Candidate text length must be measured in words rather than characters, with a strict eighty to two hundred twenty word range per lesson. Character-based limits are misleading because dense technical prose can convey meaning in fewer characters than verbose natural language. Word counts correlate better with semantic content density. The 09A and 09B fronts enforced this rule and the 09C front continues it. Each candidate must contain enough text to be retrievable and meaningful but not so much that it overwhelms the embedding model or retrieval results. The validation script splits the text on whitespace and asserts the word count falls within the range. Candidates that are too short risk being generic or lacking operational value. Candidates that are too long may be truncated or may dilute retrieval precision.
summary: Candidate text must be 80-220 words, measured by word count not characters

text: Each candidate must explicitly declare safety flags for raw chain-of-thought exposure, secrets exposure, trading execution detection, and review requirement status. The candidate schema includes boolean fields for each of these dimensions. Validation rejects any candidate that sets raw_cot_exposed, secrets_exposed, or trading_execution_detected to true. These flags make safety decisions explicit and auditable rather than implicit. The 08B promotion tool tests specifically verify that candidates with these flags set to true are rejected. The 09B front required all twelve candidates to declare false for every flag. The 09C front extends this requirement to twenty-four candidates. Safety flags are also written to the promotion audit trail, creating a permanent record that each promoted candidate was explicitly cleared of these risks before entering canonical memory.
summary: Candidates must declare safety flags for CoT, secrets, trading, and review

text: Validation must check for duplicate exact text against canonical memory and against previous ingestion batches. The 09B front performed this check by loading all 09A candidate texts and asserting that no 09B candidate had identical text. The same principle applies to 09C against both 09A and 09B. Duplicate text detection uses exact string comparison after stripping whitespace, because near-duplicate text with minor wording differences is a separate concern handled by semantic deduplication. Cross-batch duplicate checking prevents the same operational lesson from being promoted under different candidate IDs in multiple fronts. This is especially important when fronts cover related topics such as auth hardening, memory hygiene, and scaling rules. The validation script should report which candidate failed the duplicate check and which prior candidate it matched.
summary: Check duplicate exact text across current batch and all prior batches

text: Normalized text hashes must be unique within the batch before promotion. The 08F front demonstrated that thirty-six submitted entries reduced to twenty-four unique normalized texts after deduplication. Unique identifier-based deduplication alone is insufficient because different IDs can represent the same semantic content. Normalizing whitespace and case before computing SHA-256 hashes ensures consistent comparison. The validation script should compute a normalized hash for each candidate and assert that all hashes are distinct. If duplicates exist, the validation must report which candidate IDs share the same hash. This gate prevents redundant entries from entering canonical memory and degrading retrieval. The normalized text hash is also useful for future deduplication pipelines that need to compare new candidates against canonical memory without loading full text bodies into memory.
summary: Normalized text hashes must be unique within the batch before promotion

text: Temporary queue_dir promotion avoids mutating the permanent promotion_queue or semantic_staging directories. The 09A and 09B fronts used this approach by writing individual candidate JSON files into a front-local temporary directory such as tmp_agent/front_ingestion_small_batch_09b/promotion_queue_09b. The promote_candidate function accepts a queue_dir parameter that overrides the default promotion_queue path. After promotion completes, the temporary directory remains as an artifact but does not affect the canonical pipeline state. This boundary is important because the permanent promotion_queue may contain unrelated candidates from other fronts or processes. Mutating it could introduce unintended side effects or conflicts. The temporary directory also serves as an exact record of what was promoted in this front, which is useful for audit and rollback verification.
summary: Use temporary queue_dir to avoid mutating permanent promotion_queue

text: Promotion must use a supported loader path because the PromotionPipelineAdapter only recognizes standard sources such as promotion_queue directories and semantic_staging JSONL files. Front-local artifacts like curated_candidates_09b.json are not natively supported. Attempting to load them directly results in candidate_not_found errors. The correct approach is to write each candidate into a temporary queue directory that the existing loader can consume. This preserves the boundary between front artifacts and canonical pipeline state. Extending the adapter to support arbitrary JSON files would increase complexity and risk unintended loaders. The temporary queue_dir method was proven safe in 09A and 09B without any adapter modifications. Operators should verify that the loader can find candidates before requesting promotion approval tokens.
summary: Promotion must use supported loader paths; front artifacts need narrow queue_dir

text: A pre-write rollback snapshot is mandatory before the first batch promotion write. The snapshot must copy semantic_memory.jsonl, semantic_memory_faiss.index, semantic_memory_faiss_ids.json, and promotion_audit.jsonl into a timestamped directory under memory/rollback_snapshots/. It should also include the curated candidate manifest and validation summary. If any candidate fails during the batch, the system restores from this snapshot to ensure canonical memory returns to exactly the pre-promotion state. Without a snapshot, a partial batch failure would leave the index in an inconsistent state that is difficult to diagnose and repair. Snapshots should include a SNAPSHOT_REASON.txt explaining the batch context and expected increments. The 09B front created such a snapshot before promoting twelve candidates, demonstrating the pattern at small batch scale.
summary: Pre-write rollback snapshot is mandatory before first batch promotion write

text: If any candidate fails during batch promotion, the entire batch must roll back to the pre-promotion snapshot. Partial promotion leaves canonical memory in an inconsistent state where some candidates are ingested and others are not. The rollback copies snapshot files back to the canonical directory, restoring JSONL records, FAISS index, FAISS ids, and audit trail. After rollback, the system must verify that counts match the pre-promotion baseline. The 09B front used sequential promotion with per-candidate verification, breaking immediately on the first failure. This approach is safer than continuing with a partial batch because it prevents cascading errors and simplifies diagnosis. Operators should examine the failed candidate's validation errors before retrying. The promotion progress artifact records which candidates succeeded before failure, providing a complete audit trail even after rollback.
summary: Any candidate failure during batch promotion triggers full rollback

text: Post-promotion verification must prove exact JSONL, FAISS ids, and FAISS ntotal increments equal to the number of promoted candidates. For a twenty-four candidate batch starting from a baseline of seventeen seventy-one JSONL records, the expected post-promotion count is seventeen ninety-five. Similarly, FAISS ids and ntotal should increase from seventeen sixty-two to seventeen eighty-six. Assertions that check only approximate or greater-than increments are insufficient because they could mask silent failures or duplicate writes. The verify artifact should report before and after counts, the increment, and whether each matches the batch size. This contract was established in the 09A and 09B fronts and scales directly to medium batches. Exact count verification is the strongest signal that the promotion pipeline is functioning correctly.
summary: Post-promotion must prove exact JSONL, FAISS ids, and ntotal increments

text: Every promoted candidate identifier must exist in both JSONL and FAISS ids after promotion. Presence in JSONL confirms the semantic record was written to canonical memory. Presence in FAISS ids confirms the embedding was indexed. The post-promotion verification scans all JSONL records and the FAISS ids list for each candidate ID. If an ID is missing from either, the promotion pipeline has a bug that must be investigated before the front is considered complete. This check is especially important for medium batches because sequential promotion increases the chance of intermittent failures. The 09B front verified all twelve IDs in both stores. The 09C front scales this to twenty-four. Missing IDs should be reported with exact candidate identifiers and the promotion progress record for that index.
summary: Every promoted candidate ID must exist in both JSONL and FAISS ids

text: Newly promoted records must have nonblank text and no duplicate exact text within the batch. The post-promotion verification filters records to the candidate IDs promoted in this front and checks that every text field is non-empty after stripping whitespace. It then asserts that the number of unique texts equals the number of promoted records. Pre-existing blank records from older historical fronts should not cause a failure because they were introduced before the current front's governance rules. The 09B front found nine pre-existing blank records in canonical memory but confirmed that all twelve new candidates had clean text. The 09C front must apply the same policy: report pre-existing blanks as warnings but fail only if the current batch introduced them. This distinction preserves backward compatibility while maintaining quality gates.
summary: Newly promoted records must have nonblank text and no batch duplicates

text: Retrieval end-to-end should query by meaningful text phrases and require promoted candidates to appear in the top-k results. The 09B front achieved twelve out of twelve retrievals in the top five, with eleven ranking first. For a twenty-four candidate medium batch, the retrieval contract should require all twenty-four candidates to appear in the top ten results. Querying by candidate identifier tests only structural presence, not embedding quality. Meaningful phrases extracted from candidate text confirm that the embedding model captured semantic content. The retrieval artifact should report each candidate's rank, score, and whether it passed. Scores above zero point seven indicate strong semantic alignment. Retrieval failure for even one candidate should block front completion because it indicates an embedding or indexing defect that could affect agent behavior.
summary: Retrieval E2E must query by text phrase and require top-k presence

text: Retrieval failures should be reported precisely and should block completion if the required pass count is not met. The retrieval policy distinguishes between two failure modes. If a candidate is present in JSONL and FAISS ids but not retrievable by text phrase, the embedding or indexing pipeline has a defect. This is a hard failure that prevents front completion. If retrieval is partial due to low semantic similarity, the exact candidate ID, query phrase, and top-k results should be recorded for operator review. The 09B front required twelve out of twelve retrievals to pass. The 09C front maintains the same strict policy at twenty-four. Operators should not bypass retrieval failures by lowering thresholds or accepting partial results because this would allow defective embeddings into canonical memory where they degrade agent responses.
summary: Retrieval failures block completion and must report exact candidate and query

text: Agent-use probes after ingestion must use strict token authentication and read_only mode. The 09B front probed Agent V2 by posting to the chat endpoint with a valid brain token and mode set to read_only. Each probe returned HTTP two hundred with coherent answers reflecting newly promoted lessons. Using read_only mode ensures that even if the agent attempts to invoke a write tool, the ToolGateway blocks it. This is a critical safety boundary: verification should never mutate canonical memory, trigger promotions, or execute trading. Auth headers must be present on every probe because the hardened endpoints require them. The 09C front should expand agent-use probes to eight questions covering medium batch lessons, baseline helpers, and scaling boundaries. Probes should verify that the agent can retrieve and articulate lessons without executing any side effects.
summary: Agent probes must use strict token auth and read_only mode

text: Agent-use probes must confirm that no write tools, promotions, ingestion, or trading actions were executed during verification. The 09B front explicitly probed this by invoking promotion_candidate_promote in read_only mode and asserting that the ToolGateway blocked it. This test should be repeated in 09C with the same expectation. Additionally, the agent probe should verify that chat responses do not contain instructions to write files, promote candidates, or execute trades. The probe artifact records whether write tools were used, whether memory was mutated, and whether auth was required. If any probe triggers a write action, the front must halt and investigate because read_only mode should be absolute. The combination of auth and read_only mode gates provides defense in depth against accidental or malicious mutation during routine verification.
summary: Agent probes must confirm no write tools or promotions executed

text: Promotion mutates local runtime memory, but Git safety must prove that no memory files are staged or tracked. After every batch promotion, the operator must run git status and verify that memory files appear as untracked or ignored rather than staged or modified. The guard script provides automated enforcement by inspecting staged files and failing if any sensitive path is added, modified, or copied. For medium batches of twenty-four candidates, the risk of accidental staging increases because more files may be created during promotion artifacts and snapshots. The 09C front should add a dedicated Git safety phase that runs after promotion, retrieval, and agent probes. This phase checks staged files, tracked files, promotion_queue mutation, and semantic_staging mutation. Only after Git safety passes should the operator stage test and report artifacts for commit.
summary: Git safety must prove no memory files staged after runtime mutation

text: Successful twenty-four record medium batch ingestion still does not authorize mass ingestion. Large batch ingestion requires a separate front with enhanced validation, deduplication, and compaction procedures. The governance ladder is: single record, three record controlled E2E, twelve record small batch, twenty-four record medium batch, and then large controlled batch. Each stage must pass promotion, retrieval, and agent-use probes before the next stage is authorized. Jumping directly from medium to mass ingestion risks exceeding validation capacity, corrupting the index, and losing rollback granularity. The 09C front should document this boundary explicitly in its final report and recommend the next front as large controlled batch rather than mass ingestion. Operators must treat each stage as a gate that refines pipeline stability before increasing load.
summary: Successful 24-record medium batch does not authorize mass ingestion
